newsitem.title: UK: Corporate investors increase influence at Lloyd's.
newsitem.headline: Corporate investors increase influence at Lloyd's.

text.p: The increasing influence of corporate investors at Lloyd's of London was underlined on Wednesday with news that they will have an extra seat on the insurance market's ruling Council from 1998.

Despite the greater role for corporate members, Lloyd's has watered down its original proposals and gone some way to meeting concerns among Names -- the traditional backers of the market -- about their future at Lloyd's.

The Council is to set up an independent review of representation and voting arrangements before the 1998 elections and has dropped plans that one of the external Names' seats on its ruling Council should be vacated in favour of a second corporate capital representative.
Instead, an additional seat will be created for corporate investors.
Today's move is designed to reflect the greatly increased share of capacity represented by corporate members.

In 1994, the Sheldon report recommended that one seat should be reserved for a corporate member and the proportion reserved reviewed when their share reached one third of total capacity, calculated by reference to all unclosed years of account.
On that basis, the corporate share has now reached 31.5 percent but corporate members already represent 44 percent of 1997 capacity. That is expected to rise to more than 50 percent in 1998.

At present the Council of Lloyd's has five external members (individual names who do not work in the market), one representative of a corporate capital Name, six working Names (market practitioners) and six nominated members.
News of the creation of an additional seat and launch of a further review was welcomed by the Association of Lloyd's Members (ALM).
Sir David Berriman, chairman of the ALM, said it would ease the anxiety of Names that their level of representation was threatened.
The proposed review should allow the development of a method of representation that protects the rights of all, he added.
The ALM was violently opposed to the original plans to replace a Name on the Council with a corporate member and had called for a full review of the Sheldon report's recommendations.
That call appears to have been heeded.

The ALM argued that the changing nature of the market's capital providers, and in particular the evolution of dedicated corporate vehicles, means corporates are often aligned with managers of capital, rather than with capital providers, as in the case of spread vehicles which supply capital to a range of market syndicates.
Following the review, adjustments to the size and composition of the Council will be made through the 1998 and subsequent elections to reflect its recommendations.
Five members of the Council - two external and three working representatives - are standing down this year meaning elections for a total of six seats.
Those include Lloyd's chairman Sir David Rowland who retires at the end of December having completed five years in the post.
Max Taylor, executive director at Willis Corroon has been nominated by the Council to succeed Rowland, subject to his election as a working member of the council.
The elections will take place on November 7.
